newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania parliament votes to put elections on track.
newsitem.headline: Albania parliament votes to put elections on track.

text.p: Albania seemed set for new elections after European envoy Franz Vranitzky persuaded parliament to pass a fresh electoral law on Friday to get the vital polls back on track.

The elections are seen as a key element to prevent more unrest in Albania, which exploded into an orgy of violence in February and March after thousands of people lost their life savings when pyramid investment schemes collapsed.

It was Vranitzky's fifth trip to Albania since the violence erupted and his second in a week as he fulfilled the role of special envoy for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to the troubled Balkan nation.
Vranitzky was forced into his latest mission to persuade politicians to revise electoral legislation after most political parties threatened to boycott the planned elections.
These parties said an earlier electoral law passed on Monday favoured President Sali Berisha's former ruling Democratic Party.
After a sitting that lasted well into the early hours of Friday, parliament finally passed the new law.
Democratic Party chairman Tritan Shehu said the law incorporated Vranitzky's recommendations and that the elections would take place as planned on June 29.
No immediate comment was available from other parties on whether they would participate in the elections.
Vranitzky decided to stay in Albania to make sure the deal stuck after an agreement last week unravelled almost as soon as he left the country.
"I have continuously stressed that free and fair elections are the only resolution to the continuous political, economical and security crisis Albania is facing," he said.
Vranitzky spent all of Thursday trying to persuade politicians, including Berisha and Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, to find a compromise over the electoral law.
Berisha has still to formally sign a decree calling the elections.
Vranitzky warned the politicians that Albania was under close international scrutiny.

"I very clearly said to political leaders...that further delays as far as a compromise on the elections is concerned will not improve the situation and will put into question the international community's willingness to provide economic and financial support," he told a news conference on Thursday.
The deal over the electoral law was thrashed out as an explosion at an ammunition dump in southern Albania underlined the volatile situation in the country.

Three men were missing and presumed dead after the blast, which caused a huge crater at the dump near the town of Gjirokaster, said an Italian spokesman for the multinational force tasked with protecting aid supplies in Albania.

Vranitzky said that if the compromise deal was not respected, the OSCE, the Council of Europe and other international bodies would reconsider their commitment to monitor the elections to ensure they were free and fair.
At parliament, a long statement was handed out with the details of how the electoral law should be amended, setting out the division of proportional representation and majority voting.
The Democratic Party wanted more seats decided by majority vote, while other parties, led by the Socialists, favoured more allocated on a proportional basis.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were flawed.
